extracted.intended_audience: students and teachers of mathematics (learners practicing problem solving)
extracted.subtask_description: Guidance for approaching and solving mathematical problems using George Polya's four-step heuristic: understand the problem, devise a plan, carry out the plan, and look back. Includes specific prompts and a list of example strategies to use when devising a plan.

rubrics_metrics.name: Understand the problem
rubrics_metrics.description: Polya’s First Principle: Understand the problem.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Questions and checks to ensure comprehension: "Do you understand all the words used in stating the problem?" "What are you asked to find or show?" "Can you restate the problem in your own words?" "Can you think of a picture or diagram that might help you understand the problem?" "Is there enough information to enable you to find a solution?" Additional prompts from the expanded list: identify the unknown, the data, and the condition; ask whether the condition is sufficient/insufficient/redundant/contradictory; draw a figure; introduce suitable notation; separate parts of the condition and try to write them down. Emphasizes that failure to fully understand the problem is a common cause of being unable to solve it.

rubrics_metrics.name: Devise a plan
rubrics_metrics.description: Polya’s Second Principle: Devise a plan. Choose an appropriate strategy to connect the data to the unknown; many reasonable strategies exist and skill improves with practice.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Includes a partial list of specific strategies: "Guess and check", "Make an orderly list", "Eliminate possibilities", "Use symmetry", "Consider special cases", "Use direct reasoning", "Solve an equation", "Look for a pattern", "Draw a picture", "Solve a simpler problem", "Use a model", "Work backwards", "Use a formula", "Be ingenious". Expanded prompts: find the connection between the data and the unknown; consider auxiliary problems if no immediate connection; ask "Have you seen it before?"; use related problems, theorems, or methods; look at the unknown and try to match it to familiar problems; ask whether you can use a previously solved related problem (its result or method), possibly by introducing auxiliary elements; try restating the problem in different ways and revisit definitions; if stuck, attempt related problems (more accessible, more general, more special, analogous, or parts of the problem); keep only part of the condition to see how the unknown varies; consider deriving something useful from the data or changing the unknown/data so they are closer together; check whether you used all the data and all essential notions involved in the problem. Guidance emphasizes experimentation with many approaches and deliberate search for connections.

rubrics_metrics.name: Carry out the plan
rubrics_metrics.description: Polya’s Third Principle: Carry out the plan.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Execute the chosen plan with care and patience. "Carrying out your plan of the solution, check each step. Can you see clearly that the step is correct? Can you prove that it is correct?" Persist with a plan, but if it continues not to work, discard it and choose another. Warns that this iterative process (persisting, checking, switching plans) reflects how mathematics is done even by professionals.

rubrics_metrics.name: Look back
rubrics_metrics.description: Polya’s Fourth Principle: Look back. Reflect on the solution and the process after solving the problem.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Suggested checks and reflective prompts: "Can you check the result? Can you check the argument?" "Can you derive the solution differently? Can you see it at a glance?" "Can you use the result, or the method, for some other problem?" Reflection helps consolidate learning and enables predicting which strategy to use for future problems; taking time to look back yields insights into what worked and what didn't.
